name: Ostend
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Ostend | Offshore Wind & Fishing
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging in Ostend for offshore wind vessels, crew transfer vessels and beam trawlers: hull, deck and tank UTM, plus shiplift dockings.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement in Ostend for Offshore Wind, Fishing and Workboats
intro: Ostend is Belgium's offshore wind port: installation ships stage turbine components at its heavy-load terminal, and crew transfer and service vessels sail from its harbour to the wind farms on the Belgian sandbanks. Beam trawlers land at the fish auction, research and government vessels are based here, and IDP Shipyard lifts workboats and fishing vessels out of the water for repair. Ships stay long enough for gauging during mobilisations, crew rotations and dockings. For every job, our technicians make the journey from India to the vessel.

highlights.h: Crew transfer vessels on the Belgian banks
highlights.p: Aluminium and steel crew transfer vessels run out to the offshore wind farms in suitable weather almost every day. Bow fender zones, hull plating and welded joints that flex in the short North Sea chop are gauged and crack-checked when a vessel is rotated out or lifted for maintenance.

The REBO terminal gives installation and crane vessels priority berths on a reinforced heavy-load quay. Mobilisation and demobilisation open up deck areas, crane pedestals and tanks that cannot be reached during a campaign, and that is the moment to measure them.

highlights.h: Beam trawlers and the fish auction
highlights.p: Ostend's beam trawlers land their catch at the auction and lie alongside between trips. Hull plating along the waterline, gallows and derrick foundations and fish-hold structure can be gauged while the vessel is in port, or during a haul-out at the local yard.

port.h: Ostend's harbour, its sandbanks and its blue-economy traffic
p: Ostend lies on the Belgian coast west of Zeebrugge, with an entrance between breakwaters and a dredged channel through the shallow sandbanks that line the Flemish coast. The commercial port is tidal, and its approach is shaped by those banks, so ships of deeper draught plan their arrival with the tide while the smaller craft that make up most of the traffic are far less constrained. Behind the town, older inner docks connect through locks with the canal network leading to Bruges and Ghent, used by inland vessels and pleasure craft. The port is modest in scale beside Zeebrugge or Antwerp, and it has turned that into a focus: instead of competing for container or car traffic, Ostend has made itself a base for offshore energy, fishing and specialised maritime services.

The decision to make Ostend an offshore wind hub has shaped its quays. The REBO heavy-load terminal was built for installation work, with a reinforced quay and a strengthened seabed in front of it so that installation and crane vessels can load foundations, turbine parts and cables, and it now also handles heavy project cargo and components from decommissioned turbines. Operators of the wind farms in the Belgian North Sea run maintenance bases from the port, and their crew transfer vessels and service ships head out each morning when the weather allows. A hydrogen refuelling station for offshore wind vessels has opened in the port, a sign of how the fleet itself is changing. Cruise and ro-ro calls, project cargo and bulk add to the mix.

Fishing and public service fleets complete the picture. Ostend is a historic fishing port, and beam trawlers and smaller fishing vessels land at the Flemish fish auction, then lie alongside between trips. The Flemish government's pilot and survey craft and research vessels working in the North Sea use the port as a base. IDP Shipyard, founded in the 1920s to look after cod-fishing vessels, now spends much of its time on crew transfer vessels and offshore workboats, docking them on two shiplifts that lead straight into covered sheds. For gauging, Ostend therefore offers small and mid-sized steel and aluminium vessels in port on predictable schedules, plus larger installation ships during the periods when they mobilise or demobilise at the terminal.

facilities.h: Shiplifts, terminals and quays for gauging in Ostend
p: IDP Shipyard is the docking option inside the port. Its two shiplifts raise vessels out of the water and move them into covered sheds, where hull, deck and internal structure can be gauged under cover alongside repair and maintenance work. The lifts are sized for small and mid-sized vessels such as crew transfer vessels, fishing vessels, tugs, pilot boats and many workboats, and the yard also supports mobilisation and demobilisation work on installation ships berthed in the port. Larger offshore vessels and cargo ships that need a drydock go to bigger yards elsewhere in the region, and a pre-docking gauging in Ostend can set their steel list before they sail.

Afloat gauging centres on the REBO terminal, the service vessel berths and the fishing harbour. Installation vessels at REBO are best measured during mobilisation or demobilisation, when deck cargo and sea-fastenings are out of the way and the crew can open tanks. Service operation and crew transfer vessels berth in the port between shifts, so work on them is planned around crew rotations and maintenance days rather than one long stop. Fishing vessels lie at the quays between trips and can be measured there, and the research and government vessels based in Ostend have planned maintenance periods that suit a structured gauging programme.
list: IDP Shipyard shiplifts and covered sheds — docking and renewal survey gauging on crew transfer vessels, fishing vessels, tugs and workboats, under cover.
REBO heavy-load terminal — deck plating, crane pedestals, sea-fastening areas and tanks on installation and crane vessels during mobilisation.
Service vessel berths — gangway and crane foundations, deck structure and ballast tanks on service operation vessels during crew rotations.
Fishing harbour quays — hull, gallows foundation and fish-hold readings on beam trawlers lying alongside between trips.
Research and government vessel berths — structured gauging programmes fitted into planned maintenance periods.

context.h: Belgian rules, offshore wind growth and the Ostend fleet
p: Port state control in Ostend is exercised by the Federal Public Service Mobility and Transport under the Paris MoU, the same authority that inspects ships calling at Zeebrugge and Antwerp. Much of the Ostend fleet, however, is checked as often by its charterers as by any authority. Wind farm owners and turbine makers audit crew transfer and service vessels before and during contracts, and fishing vessels are surveyed under their flag state's safety rules. A structural record built on recent thickness readings helps a vessel through each of these checks, and it is far easier to assemble during a planned haul-out than in a hurry before an audit.

Belgian offshore wind is set to grow further with the Princess Elisabeth Zone, the country's second offshore wind area, so Ostend expects more installation, cable and service traffic in the coming years. The fleet serving the existing farms is also getting older: many crew transfer vessels have been working the Belgian banks for years, and their owners have to decide whether to refit, re-engine or replace them as charterers raise their standards and lower-emission designs, including hydrogen-fuelled vessels, come into service. Gauging the hulls of the existing boats is a practical first step in each of those decisions.

jobs.h: UTM jobs we see at Ostend
jobs.p: Ostend work is mostly on small and mid-sized offshore and fishing vessels, with occasional larger installation ships. Owners of crew transfer vessels want gauging and crack detection that can be done during a haul-out at the yard or spread over maintenance days without losing charter time. Installation vessel superintendents want structure measured in the short gap between campaigns. Fishing vessel owners ask for hull gauging at a docking or before a sale, and government and research operators plan gauging into their maintenance periods. Aluminium hulls need the gauge set up for the material, with crack checks done by dye penetrant. Examples:
list: A crew transfer vessel lifted at IDP Shipyard: hull plating, fender zone and keel areas gauged and aluminium welds checked by dye penetrant during scheduled maintenance.
A jack-up installation vessel at the REBO terminal: deck plating, crane pedestal welds by MPI and preload tank gauging during demobilisation.
A beam trawler before sale: shell plating along the waterline and bilge, gallows and derrick foundations and fish-hold structure gauged for the buyer.
A service operation vessel between rotations: gangway foundation, deck structure and ballast tank readings taken in planned sections.
A research or survey vessel in its maintenance period: shell, tank and sea chest gauging for an intermediate or renewal survey.

logistics: Brussels Airport is the usual international arrival point, with direct trains from Brussels to Ostend; Ostend-Bruges Airport handles only a limited number of flights. Access to the REBO terminal, the shipyard and the fishing harbour is controlled, and the ship's agent or the yard registers the team in advance. Technicians travel from India on Schengen visas, which need time to obtain, so the earlier we know the haul-out date or the demobilisation window, the more smoothly the team can be booked onto the right day.

faqs.q: How do you gauge aluminium crew transfer vessels in Ostend?
faqs.a: With the same ultrasonic method as steel, but the gauge is calibrated on an aluminium reference because sound travels through aluminium at a different velocity. Crack detection on aluminium uses dye penetrant, since magnetic particle testing only works on magnetic steels. The bow fender zone, hull plating near the waterline and welded connections that flex in a short sea are where we concentrate.

faqs.q: Can a vessel be docked in Ostend for a renewal survey?
faqs.a: Small and mid-sized vessels can, on IDP Shipyard's shiplifts, which move them into covered sheds; the team gauges there alongside the class surveyor and the yard. Larger ships, including most installation vessels and cargo ships, dock at bigger yards elsewhere in the region and can be gauged in Ostend beforehand so that the steel list is ready.

faqs.q: Can installation vessels be gauged at the REBO terminal?
faqs.a: Yes, ideally during mobilisation or demobilisation, when sea-fastenings and deck cargo are off and tanks can be opened. We agree the scope with the superintendent and the terminal so that gauging fits around crane work and loading. Crack detection on crane pedestals and deck welds is often added in the same visit.

faqs.q: Can a fishing vessel be gauged between trips?
faqs.a: Yes. Beam trawlers usually spend a short time in port between trips, which allows deck and accessible hull readings, and the fish hold once it has been emptied and cleaned. A full hull survey that includes bottom plating needs the vessel lifted at the yard. Owners often combine the two, starting alongside and completing the programme at the next haul-out.
